meta.sourceDocument: Cambridge International AS & A Level Chemistry 9701 syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027 (version 1, September 2022)
meta.validFor: Exams in 2025, 2026 and 2027 (June and November series; March series in India)
meta.representation: Official 2025-2027 syllabus hierarchy with normalized, source-checked numbered learning outcomes for Topics 1-37.
meta.sourceVerification: Whole subject-content layer cross-checked against the official Cambridge 9701 2025-2027 syllabus PDF; normalized wording is intentionally not a verbatim copy.

topics.title: Particles in the atom and atomic radius
outcomes: Understand that atoms are mostly empty space surrounding a very small, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells around the nucleus.
Identify and describe protons, neutrons and electrons by their relative charges and masses.
Understand atomic number, proton number, mass number and nucleon number.
Describe the distribution of mass and charge within an atom.
Describe the behaviour of proton, neutron and electron beams moving at the same velocity in an electric field.
Determine the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions from atomic/proton number, mass/nucleon number and charge.
State and explain qualitatively the variations in atomic and ionic radii across a period and down a group.

topics.title: Isotopes
outcomes: Define an isotope in terms of its numbers of protons and neutrons.
Understand isotope notation using mass/nucleon number and atomic/proton number.
Explain why isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties.
Explain why isotopes of the same element have different physical properties, limited to mass and density.

topics.title: Electrons, energy levels and atomic orbitals
outcomes: Understand shells, sub-shells, orbitals, principal quantum number n and ground state as applied to electronic configuration.
Describe the number of orbitals and maximum electrons in s, p and d sub-shells.
Describe the order of increasing sub-shell energy within the first three shells and the 4s and 4p sub-shells.
Describe electronic configurations by shell, sub-shell and orbital.
Explain electronic configurations in terms of electron energy and inter-electron repulsion.
Determine electronic configurations of atoms and ions from proton number and charge using full or shorthand notation.
Understand and use electrons-in-boxes notation.
Describe and sketch the shapes of s and p orbitals.
Describe a free radical as a species with one or more unpaired electrons.

topics.title: Ionisation energy
outcomes: Define and use first ionisation energy, IE.
Construct equations representing first, second and subsequent ionisation energies.
Identify and explain trends in ionisation energies across periods and down groups.
Identify and explain variation in successive ionisation energies of an element.
Understand ionisation energies as arising from attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron.
Explain ionisation-energy factors using nuclear charge, atomic/ionic radius, shielding and spin-pair repulsion.
Deduce electronic configurations from successive ionisation-energy data.
Deduce an element's position in the Periodic Table from successive ionisation-energy data.

sections.title: Atoms, molecules and stoichiometry
sections.summary: Atoms, molecules and stoichiometry. 4 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: Relative masses of atoms and molecules
outcomes: Define the unified atomic mass unit as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Define relative atomic mass, relative isotopic mass, relative molecular mass and relative formula mass in terms of the unified atomic mass unit.

topics.title: The mole and the Avogadro constant
outcomes: Define and use the mole in terms of the Avogadro constant.

topics.title: Formulas
outcomes: Write ionic-compound formulas from ionic charges and oxidation numbers, including predicting ionic charge from Periodic Table position and recalling the specified common ions.
Write and construct balanced equations, including ionic equations without spectator ions, and use appropriate state symbols.
Define and use empirical and molecular formula.
Understand and use anhydrous, hydrated and water of crystallisation.
Calculate empirical and molecular formulas from given data.

topics.title: Reacting masses and volumes (of solutions and gases)
outcomes: Perform mole calculations involving reacting masses and percentage yield, gas volumes, solution volumes and concentrations, and limiting and excess reagents.
Deduce stoichiometric relationships from mole calculations.

topics.title: Electronegativity and bonding
outcomes: Define electronegativity as the power of an atom to attract electrons to itself.
Explain factors influencing electronegativity using nuclear charge, atomic radius and shielding by inner shells and sub-shells.
State and explain electronegativity trends across a period and down a group.
Use Pauling electronegativity differences to predict ionic or covalent bonding.

topics.title: Ionic bonding
outcomes: Define ionic bonding as electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Describe ionic bonding using sodium chloride, magnesium oxide and calcium fluoride as examples.

topics.title: Metallic bonding
outcomes: Define metallic bonding as electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

topics.title: Covalent bonding and coordinate (dative covalent) bonding
outcomes: Define covalent bonding as electrostatic attraction between two nuclei and a shared pair of electrons, and describe covalent bonding in the specified molecules and expanded-octet examples.
Describe coordinate (dative covalent) bonding, including formation of NH4+ from ammonia and hydrogen chloride and bonding in Al2Cl6.
Describe sigma and pi bonds using orbital overlap, apply them to H2, C2H6, C2H4, HCN and N2, use sp/sp2/sp3 hybridisation, and relate bond energy and bond length to covalent reactivity.

topics.title: Shapes of molecules
outcomes: State and explain molecular shapes and bond angles using VSEPR theory for the specified examples.
Predict shapes and bond angles in molecules and ions analogous to the specified VSEPR examples.

topics.title: Intermolecular forces, electronegativity and bond properties
outcomes: Describe hydrogen bonding in molecules containing N-H and O-H groups and use it to explain anomalous properties of water.
Use electronegativity to explain bond polarity and molecular dipole moments.
Describe van der Waals' forces, including instantaneous dipole-induced dipole and permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces, including hydrogen bonding.
State that ionic, covalent and metallic bonding are generally stronger than intermolecular forces.

topics.title: Dot-and-cross diagrams
outcomes: Use dot-and-cross diagrams to illustrate ionic, covalent and coordinate bonding, including species with expanded octets or odd numbers of electrons.

sections.title: States of matter
sections.summary: States of matter. 2 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: The gaseous state: ideal and real gases and pV = nRT
outcomes: Explain the origin of gas pressure in terms of collisions between gas molecules and container walls.
Understand that an ideal gas has negligible particle volume and no intermolecular attractions.
Use pV = nRT in calculations, including determination of relative molecular mass.

topics.title: Bonding and structure
outcomes: Describe the lattice structures of giant ionic, simple molecular, giant molecular and giant metallic crystalline solids, using the specified examples.
Describe, interpret and predict how structure and bonding affect melting point, boiling point, electrical conductivity and solubility.
Deduce the structure and bonding of a substance from given information.

topics.title: Enthalpy change, ΔH
outcomes: Understand that chemical reactions involve enthalpy changes and can be exothermic or endothermic.
Construct and interpret reaction pathway diagrams showing reaction enthalpy change and activation energy.
Define and use standard conditions and the specified enthalpy-change terms: reaction, formation, combustion and neutralisation.
Understand energy transfer during reactions as arising from breaking and making chemical bonds.
Use bond energies to calculate enthalpy changes of reaction.
Understand that some bond energies are exact while others are average values.
Calculate enthalpy changes from experimental results using q = mcΔT and ΔH = -mcΔT/n.

topics.title: Hess’s law
outcomes: Apply Hess's law to construct simple energy cycles.
Use energy cycles and relevant energy terms to calculate enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly and to use bond-energy data.

topics.title: Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)
outcomes: Calculate oxidation numbers of elements in compounds and ions.
Use changes in oxidation numbers to help balance chemical equations.
Explain and use redox, oxidation, reduction and disproportionation in terms of electron transfer and oxidation-number changes.
Explain and use oxidising agent and reducing agent.
Use Roman numerals to indicate oxidation-number magnitude.

topics.title: Chemical equilibria: reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium
outcomes: Understand reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium as equal forward and reverse rates with constant concentrations, and the need for a closed system.
Define Le Chatelier's principle and use it to deduce qualitative equilibrium shifts caused by temperature, concentration, pressure or catalysts.
Deduce Kc expressions and carry out Kc calculations.
Use mole fraction and partial pressure and deduce Kp expressions.
Use Kc and Kp expressions for calculations without requiring quadratic equations.
Calculate equilibrium quantities from appropriate data.
State whether temperature, concentration, pressure or a catalyst changes the equilibrium constant.
Describe and explain Haber-process and Contact-process conditions as applications of dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle.

topics.title: Brønsted–Lowry theory of acids and bases
outcomes: State the specified common acids and their formulas.
State the specified common alkalis and their formulas.
Describe the Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases.
Describe strong acids/bases as fully dissociated and weak acids/bases as partially dissociated in aqueous solution.
Relate pH 7 to neutral water and distinguish acidic and alkaline solution pH ranges.
Explain qualitative differences between strong and weak acids, including reaction with a reactive metal and differences in pH measured by pH meter, universal indicator or conductivity.
Understand neutralisation as H+(aq) and OH-(aq) forming H2O(l).
Understand that salts are formed in neutralisation reactions.
Sketch pH titration curves for combinations of strong and weak acids with strong and weak alkalis.
Select suitable indicators for acid-alkali titrations from given data.

topics.title: Rate of reaction
outcomes: Explain and use rate of reaction, collision frequency, effective collisions and non-effective collisions.
Explain qualitatively how concentration and pressure affect reaction rate through the frequency of effective collisions.
Use experimental data to calculate reaction rate.

topics.title: Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy
outcomes: Define activation energy, EA, as the minimum energy required for an effective collision.
Sketch and use the Boltzmann distribution to explain the significance of activation energy.
Explain qualitatively how temperature changes reaction rate using the Boltzmann distribution and frequency of effective collisions.

topics.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts
outcomes: Explain catalyst and catalysis, including that a catalyst provides a different mechanism with lower activation energy, the Boltzmann-distribution explanation, and reaction-pathway diagrams with and without an effective catalyst.

sections.title: The Periodic Table: chemical periodicity
sections.summary: The Periodic Table: chemical periodicity. 3 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: Periodicity of physical properties of the elements in Period 3
outcomes: Describe qualitative periodic variations in atomic radius, ionic radius, melting point and electrical conductivity across Period 3.
Explain melting-point and electrical-conductivity variation in terms of structure and bonding.

topics.title: Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3
outcomes: Describe and write equations for Period 3 element reactions with oxygen, chlorine and water where specified.
State and explain oxidation-number variation in specified Period 3 oxides and chlorides using outer-shell electrons.
Describe and write equations for reactions of specified Period 3 oxides with water and identify likely solution pH.
Describe, explain and write equations for acid-base behaviour of specified Period 3 oxides and hydroxides, including relevant amphoteric behaviour.
Describe, explain and write equations for reactions of specified Period 3 chlorides with water and identify likely solution pH.
Explain trends in Period 3 chemical properties using bonding and electronegativity.
Suggest bonding types in specified chlorides and oxides from chemical and physical properties.

topics.title: Chemical periodicity of other elements
outcomes: Predict characteristic properties of an element in a given group using chemical periodicity.
Deduce the nature, possible Periodic Table position and identity of unknown elements from physical and chemical property data.

topics.title: Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals, magnesium to barium, and their compounds
outcomes: Describe and write equations for Group 2 elements reacting with oxygen, water and dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids.
Describe and write equations for Group 2 oxides, hydroxides and carbonates reacting with water and dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids.
Describe and write equations for thermal decomposition of Group 2 nitrates and carbonates, including the trend in thermal stability.
Describe and predict trends in physical and chemical properties of the Group 2 elements and their compounds.
State the variation in solubilities of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates.

topics.title: Physical properties of the Group 17 elements
outcomes: Describe the colours and volatility trend of chlorine, bromine and iodine.
Describe and explain the trend in bond strength of halogen molecules.
Interpret volatility in terms of instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces.

topics.title: The chemical properties of the halogen elements and the hydrogen halides
outcomes: Describe relative reactivity of halogen elements as oxidising agents.
Describe reactions of halogen elements with hydrogen and explain their relative reactivity.
Describe relative thermal stabilities of hydrogen halides and explain them using bond strengths.

topics.title: Some reactions of the halide ions
outcomes: Describe relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents.
Describe and explain halide-ion reactions with aqueous silver ions followed by aqueous ammonia and with concentrated sulfuric acid, including balanced equations.

topics.title: The reactions of chlorine
outcomes: Describe and interpret chlorine reactions with cold and hot aqueous sodium hydroxide in terms of oxidation-number changes and identify them as disproportionation.
Explain, including with an equation, the use of chlorine in water purification, including formation of HOCl and ClO- active species.

sections.title: Nitrogen and sulfur
sections.summary: Nitrogen and sulfur. 1 official syllabus subsection.

topics.title: Nitrogen and sulfur
outcomes: Explain nitrogen's low reactivity using triple-bond strength and lack of polarity.
Describe and explain ammonia basicity, ammonium-ion structure and formation, and displacement of ammonia from ammonium salts using acid-base reactions.
State and explain natural and man-made occurrences of nitrogen oxides and their catalytic removal from internal-combustion-engine exhaust.
Understand that NO and NO2 can react with unburned hydrocarbons to form PAN, a component of photochemical smog.
Describe the role of NO and NO2 in acid-rain formation, including catalytic oxidation of atmospheric sulfur dioxide.

sections.title: An introduction to AS Level organic chemistry
sections.summary: An introduction to AS Level organic chemistry. 4 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: Formulas, functional groups and the naming of organic compounds
outcomes: Define hydrocarbons as compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only.
Recognise alkanes as simple hydrocarbons without a functional group.
Understand that functional groups largely determine the physical and chemical properties of the listed organic classes.
Interpret general, structural, displayed and skeletal formulae for the specified organic classes.
Use systematic nomenclature for simple aliphatic compounds with the stated carbon-number limits.
Deduce molecular and/or empirical formulae from structural, displayed or skeletal formulae.

topics.title: Characteristic organic reactions
outcomes: Use terminology for homologous series, saturated/unsaturated compounds, homolytic/heterolytic fission, radicals, nucleophiles, electrophiles, addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis, condensation, oxidation and reduction.
Use terminology for free-radical substitution, electrophilic addition, nucleophilic substitution and nucleophilic addition mechanisms, including curly-arrow electron-pair notation.

topics.title: Shapes of organic molecules; σ and π bonds
outcomes: Classify organic molecules as straight-chain, branched or cyclic.
Explain molecular shapes and bond angles for sp, sp² and sp³ hybridised atoms.
Describe σ and π bond arrangements for sp, sp² and sp³ hybridisation.
Use planar correctly for appropriate organic molecules such as ethene.

topics.title: Isomerism: structural isomerism and stereoisomerism
outcomes: Distinguish chain, positional and functional-group structural isomerism.
Distinguish geometrical and optical stereoisomerism.
Explain cis/trans isomerism in alkenes through restricted rotation about π bonds.
Explain chiral centres and enantiomers.
Identify chiral centres and cis/trans isomerism from structural formulae, including cyclic compounds.
Deduce possible isomers from a known molecular formula.

topics.title: Alkanes
outcomes: Recall alkane preparation by alkene hydrogenation and cracking.
Describe complete/incomplete combustion and free-radical substitution with chlorine/bromine under UV light.
Explain initiation, propagation and termination in free-radical substitution.
Explain cracking as a route to useful lower-relative-mass alkanes and alkenes.
Explain low alkane reactivity using strong, relatively non-polar C–H bonds.
Recognise combustion pollutants and catalytic removal.

topics.title: Alkenes
outcomes: Recall alkene preparation by elimination, dehydration and cracking.
Describe alkene additions with H₂, steam, HX and X₂, specified oxidations and addition polymerisation.
Use aqueous bromine to test for C=C.
Explain electrophilic-addition mechanisms using bromine/ethene and HBr/propene.
Explain alkyl inductive effects on carbocation stability and Markovnikov addition.

topics.title: Halogenoalkanes
outcomes: Recall halogenoalkane preparation by radical substitution, alkene addition and alcohol substitution.
Classify halogenoalkanes as primary, secondary or tertiary.
Describe nucleophilic substitution with OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃ and aqueous silver nitrate.
Describe ethanolic-OH elimination to form alkenes.
Explain SN1 and SN2 mechanisms and alkyl inductive effects.
Relate halogenoalkane class to predominant SN1/SN2 pathway.
Explain reactivity differences using C–X bond strength and silver-nitrate reactions.

topics.title: Alcohols
outcomes: Recall routes to alcohols from alkenes, halogenoalkanes, carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids and esters.
Describe alcohol combustion, substitution, reaction with sodium, oxidation, dehydration and ester formation.
Classify primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols and use oxidation behaviour to distinguish them.
Identify a CH3CH(OH)– group with the alkaline iodine test.
Explain alcohol acidity relative to water.

topics.title: Aldehydes and ketones
outcomes: Recall aldehyde/ketone preparation by oxidation of primary/secondary alcohols.
Describe carbonyl reduction and hydroxynitrile formation with HCN.
Explain nucleophilic addition of HCN to carbonyl compounds.
Use 2,4-DNPH to detect carbonyl compounds.
Distinguish aldehydes and ketones using Fehling's/Tollens' tests and oxidation.
Identify CH3CO– groups using the alkaline iodine test.

sections.title: Carboxylic acids and derivatives
sections.summary: Carboxylic acids and derivatives. 2 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: Carboxylic acids
outcomes: Recall carboxylic-acid preparation by oxidation and nitrile/ester hydrolysis.
Describe reactions with reactive metals, alkalis, carbonates, alcohols and LiAlH4.

topics.title: Esters
outcomes: Recall ester formation from alcohol and carboxylic acid with concentrated H2SO4 catalyst.
Describe acid- and alkali-catalysed ester hydrolysis on heating.

topics.title: Primary amines
outcomes: Recall primary-amine preparation from halogenoalkanes using ammonia under pressure.

topics.title: Nitriles and hydroxynitriles
outcomes: Recall nitrile formation from halogenoalkanes using ethanolic cyanide.
Recall hydroxynitrile formation from carbonyl compounds with HCN/cyanide catalyst.
Describe nitrile hydrolysis to carboxylic acids.

topics.title: Addition polymerisation
outcomes: Describe addition polymerisation using poly(ethene) and PVC.
Deduce an addition-polymer repeat unit from a monomer.
Identify monomers from a polymer section.
Explain disposal difficulties of poly(alkene)s.

topics.title: Organic synthesis
outcomes: For multi-functional molecules, identify functional groups and predict properties/reactions.
Devise multi-step synthetic routes using syllabus reactions.
Analyse a synthesis by reaction type, reagents and possible by-products.

topics.title: Infrared spectroscopy
outcomes: Analyse a simple IR spectrum to identify required functional groups.

topics.title: Mass spectrometry
outcomes: Interpret mass spectra using m/e and isotope abundance.
Calculate relative atomic mass from isotope data or a mass spectrum.
Deduce organic molecular mass from the molecular-ion peak.
Suggest simple fragment identities.
Use the [M+1]+ peak to estimate carbon number.
Use [M+2]+ patterns to detect bromine/chlorine.

topics.title: Lattice energy and Born–Haber cycles
outcomes: Define atomisation enthalpy and lattice energy.
Define first electron affinity and explain its factors and Group 16/17 trends.
Construct and use Born–Haber cycles.
Perform Born–Haber calculations.
Explain ionic-charge and ionic-radius effects on lattice-energy magnitude.

topics.title: Enthalpies of solution and hydration
outcomes: Define hydration and solution enthalpy changes.
Construct/use cycles linking solution enthalpy, lattice energy and hydration enthalpy.
Calculate using these cycles.
Explain ionic-charge and ionic-radius effects on hydration enthalpy.

topics.title: Entropy change, ΔS
outcomes: Define entropy as possible arrangements of particles and their energy.
Predict/explain entropy-change signs for state changes, temperature changes and changes in gaseous-molecule number.
Calculate reaction entropy from standard entropy data.

topics.title: Gibbs free energy change, ΔG
outcomes: Use ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.
Calculate Gibbs free-energy changes.
Use the sign of ΔG to assess feasibility.
Predict temperature effects on feasibility.

topics.title: Electrolysis
outcomes: Predict electrolysis products from electrolyte state, electrode potential/redox position and concentration.
Use F = Le.
Calculate charge using Q = It and calculate mass/volume liberated.
Describe an electrolytic determination of Avogadro's constant.

topics.title: Standard electrode potentials E°; standard cell potentials E°cell and the Nernst equation
outcomes: Define standard electrode-reduction and standard cell potentials.
Describe the standard hydrogen electrode.
Describe measurement of standard electrode potentials.
Calculate standard cell potentials.
Use cell potentials for polarity, electron flow and feasibility.
Compare oxidising/reducing strengths using E°.
Construct redox equations from half-equations.
Predict concentration effects on electrode potential.
Use the Nernst equation quantitatively.
Use ΔG° = −nFE°cell.

topics.title: Acids and bases
outcomes: Use conjugate-acid/base terminology and identify pairs.
Use pH, Ka, pKa and Kw mathematically within syllabus limits.
Calculate [H+] and pH for strong acids, strong alkalis and weak acids.
Define, prepare and explain buffer solutions.
Describe buffer uses including bicarbonate in blood.
Calculate buffer pH.
Define and write Ksp expressions.
Calculate Ksp or concentrations.
Use the common-ion effect and perform related Ksp calculations.

topics.title: Partition coefficients
outcomes: Define Kpc.
Calculate/use Kpc when the solute remains in the same physical state in both solvents.
Explain Kpc in terms of solute/solvent polarity.

topics.title: Simple rate equations, orders of reaction and rate constants
outcomes: Use rate-equation terminology including order, overall order, k, half-life, rate-determining step and intermediate.
Use rate = k[A]^m[B]^n for orders 0,1,2 and deduce order from graphs/data.
Interpret concentration-time and rate-concentration graphs and calculate initial rates.
Construct rate equations.
Use first-order half-life.
Calculate k from initial rates or k = 0.693/t½.
Relate multi-step mechanisms to rate equations and identify intermediates/catalysts/rate-determining steps.
Explain temperature effects on k and rate.

topics.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts
outcomes: Distinguish homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis.
Explain heterogeneous catalysis through adsorption, bond weakening and desorption.
Explain homogeneous catalysis through catalyst use and regeneration.

topics.title: Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals, magnesium to barium, and their compounds
outcomes: Explain Group 2 thermal-stability trends for nitrates/carbonates using ionic-radius polarisation.
Explain hydroxide/sulfate solubility and solution-enthalpy trends using hydration enthalpy and lattice energy.

sections.title: Chemistry of transition elements
sections.summary: Chemistry of transition elements. 5 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: General physical and chemical properties of the first row of transition elements, titanium to copper
outcomes: Define transition elements using incomplete d orbitals in stable ions.
Sketch 3dxy and 3dz² orbitals.
Describe variable oxidation states, catalysis, complex ions and coloured compounds.
Explain variable oxidation states using 3d/4s energy similarity.
Explain catalysis using multiple oxidation states and accessible d orbitals.
Explain complex formation using accessible d orbitals.

topics.title: General characteristic chemical properties of the first set of transition elements, titanium to copper
outcomes: Describe specified transition-metal ligand complexes.
Define ligands and distinguish monodentate, bidentate and polydentate ligands.
Define complexes and describe linear, square-planar, tetrahedral and octahedral geometries.
Use coordination number to predict complex formula/charge.
Explain ligand exchange using specified Cu(II)/Co(II) systems.
Use E° to assess transition-metal redox feasibility.
Describe/calculate specified permanganate/ethanedioate, permanganate/Fe²⁺ and Cu²⁺/I⁻ systems.
Perform other supplied redox calculations.

topics.title: Colour of complexes
outcomes: Use degenerate/non-degenerate d-orbital terminology.
Explain d-orbital splitting in octahedral/tetrahedral complexes.
Explain colours via d-electron promotion and light absorption.
Explain ligand effects on ΔE and complementary colour.
Use Cu(II)/Co(II) ligand exchange to explain colour changes.

topics.title: Stereoisomerism in transition element complexes
outcomes: Describe geometrical and optical stereoisomerism in complexes, including bidentate examples.
Deduce overall polarity of specified stereoisomers.

topics.title: Stability constants, Kstab
outcomes: Define Kstab for complex formation.
Write Kstab expressions excluding water where appropriate.
Use Kstab expressions in calculations.
Explain ligand exchange using Kstab and relate large Kstab to complex stability.

sections.title: An introduction to A Level organic chemistry
sections.summary: An introduction to A Level organic chemistry. 4 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: Formulas, functional groups and the naming of organic compounds
outcomes: Understand functional-group effects on listed organic classes.
Interpret general, structural, displayed and skeletal formulae.
Use systematic nomenclature for permitted simple aliphatic/cyclic compounds.
Use systematic nomenclature for simple aromatic compounds with one benzene ring.

topics.title: Characteristic organic reactions
outcomes: Use electrophilic-substitution and addition–elimination terminology.

topics.title: Shapes of aromatic organic molecules; σ and π bonds
outcomes: Explain benzene/aromatic molecular shape using sp² hybridisation, σ bonds and a delocalised π system.

topics.title: Isomerism: optical
outcomes: Explain shared physical/chemical properties of enantiomers apart from optical rotation and possible biological activity.
Use optically active and racemic mixture terminology.

topics.title: Arenes
outcomes: Describe specified benzene/methylbenzene reactions including halogenation, nitration, Friedel–Crafts reactions, side-chain oxidation and hydrogenation.
Explain electrophilic substitution and aromatic stabilisation.
Predict side-chain versus ring halogenation from conditions.
Explain substituent directing effects for the specified groups.

topics.title: Halogenoarenes
outcomes: Recall halogenoarene formation by chlorine/bromine substitution with AlCl3/AlBr3.
Explain lower halogenoarene reactivity compared with halogenoalkanes.

topics.title: Alcohols
outcomes: Describe alcohol reaction with acyl chlorides to form esters.

topics.title: Phenol
outcomes: Recall phenol preparation by diazotisation of phenylamine followed by hydrolysis.
Describe phenol reactions with bases, sodium, diazonium salts, nitric acid and bromine.
Explain phenol acidity.
Compare water, phenol and ethanol acidity.
Explain differing nitration/bromination conditions for phenol and benzene.
Recall 2-,4-,6-directing behaviour of the phenolic OH group.
Apply phenol chemistry to related phenolic compounds.

sections.title: Carboxylic acids and derivatives
sections.summary: Carboxylic acids and derivatives. 3 official syllabus subsections.

topics.title: Carboxylic acids
outcomes: Recall benzoic-acid preparation by alkylbenzene side-chain oxidation.
Describe conversion of carboxylic acids to acyl chlorides.
Describe further oxidation of methanoic and ethanedioic acids.
Compare carboxylic-acid, phenol and alcohol acidities.
Explain chlorine-substituted carboxylic-acid acidity.

topics.title: Esters
outcomes: Recall ester formation from alcohols and acyl chlorides.

topics.title: Acyl chlorides
outcomes: Recall acyl-chloride preparation from carboxylic acids.
Describe acyl-chloride reactions with water, alcohols, phenols, ammonia and primary/secondary amines.
Explain addition–elimination.
Compare hydrolysis rates of acyl chlorides, alkyl chlorides and halogenoarenes.

topics.title: Primary and secondary amines
outcomes: Recall primary/secondary amine preparation from halogenoalkanes, amides and nitriles.
Describe amide formation from ammonia/amine and an acyl chloride.
Explain aqueous amine basicity.

topics.title: Phenylamine and azo compounds
outcomes: Describe phenylamine preparation via nitration/reduction.
Describe phenylamine reactions with bromine and nitrous acid/nitrite, including diazonium formation and hydrolysis to phenol.
Compare ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine basicity.
Describe azo coupling, identify the azo group and recognise azo dyes.

topics.title: Amides
outcomes: Recall amide formation from ammonia or primary amines and acyl chlorides.
Describe amide hydrolysis and LiAlH4 reduction.
Explain why amides are weaker bases than amines.

topics.title: Amino acids
outcomes: Explain amino-acid acid/base behaviour and zwitterions, including isoelectric point.
Describe peptide-bond formation to di- and tripeptides.
Interpret/predict electrophoresis of amino acids and dipeptides at varying pH.

topics.title: Condensation polymerisation
outcomes: Describe polyester formation from diols with dicarboxylic acids/dioyl chlorides and from hydroxycarboxylic acids.
Describe polyamide formation from diamines with dicarboxylic acids/dioyl chlorides, aminocarboxylic acids and amino acids.
Deduce condensation-polymer repeat units.
Identify monomers from condensation-polymer sections.

topics.title: Predicting the type of polymerisation
outcomes: Predict polymerisation type from monomer(s).
Deduce polymerisation type from a polymer segment.

topics.title: Degradable polymers
outcomes: Recognise why poly(alkene)s are difficult to biodegrade.
Recognise light-driven polymer degradation.
Recognise biodegradation of polyesters/polyamides by acidic or alkaline hydrolysis.

topics.title: Organic synthesis
outcomes: For multi-functional molecules, identify functional groups and predict properties/reactions.
Devise multi-step synthetic routes.
Analyse synthesis routes by reaction type, reagents and possible by-products.

topics.title: Thin-layer chromatography
outcomes: Define TLC stationary/mobile phases, Rf, solvent front and baseline.
Interpret Rf values.
Explain Rf differences using stationary-phase interactions and mobile-phase solubility.

topics.title: Gas / liquid chromatography
outcomes: Define GC stationary/mobile phases and retention time.
Interpret chromatograms for mixture composition.
Explain retention times using stationary-phase interaction.

topics.title: Carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy
outcomes: Interpret carbon-13 NMR for carbon environments and possible structures.
Predict/explain the number of carbon-13 NMR peaks.

topics.title: Proton NMR spectroscopy
outcomes: Interpret proton NMR using chemical shifts, peak areas, splitting and possible structures.
Predict proton shifts and splitting.
Describe TMS as chemical-shift standard.
Explain use of deuterated solvents.
Identify O–H/N–H protons by D2O exchange.

topics.title: Combined analytical techniques
outcomes: Use combined chromatography, IR, mass-spectrometry and NMR evidence to identify or distinguish simple organic structures.
